title: Broadcom Missed One Number by $1.2 Billion. It Triggered the Worst Chip Selloff Since 2020.
excerpt: The AI trade's tolerance for imperfection hit zero. Wipro crashed 8.4%, Korea tripped a circuit breaker, and $923 billion in semiconductor value vanished in two days.
body:
The biggest stock market rout in months did not start with a war, a central bank, or a pandemic. It started with a single number: $16 billion.

That was Broadcom's guidance for third-quarter AI semiconductor revenue — up 200 percent year-over-year, record-breaking by any normal standard, and roughly $1.2 billion below what Wall Street had expected. On June 4, Broadcom stock collapsed 12.6 percent, erasing $280 billion in market value in a single trading session. Within 48 hours, the entire AI infrastructure trade had cracked open.

## The Cascade

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped more than 10 percent in its steepest single-day fall since March 2020. The Nasdaq plunged 4.2 percent on Friday. The top 10 semiconductor decliners erased roughly $923 billion in aggregate market value. A memory chip ETF tracking SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung — which had returned 134 percent earlier this year — sank 15 percent.

By Monday morning, the carnage had reached Asia. South Korea's KOSPI plunged over 8 percent at the open, triggering a 20-minute circuit breaker — the second halt this year. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each fell more than 10 percent. Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 3.9 percent. The MSCI Asia ex-Japan index tumbled 3.5 percent.

And then it hit India.

## India Caught in the Crossfire

The Nifty 50 fell 1.04 percent to 23,123. The Sensex shed nearly 1 percent to 73,524, with both benchmarks closing at two-month lows. Fifteen of 16 major sectors declined. IT stocks — which make up a significant chunk of the benchmarks — were among the hardest hit, with the Nifty IT index falling 1.2 percent.

Wipro was the standout casualty, sliding 8.4 percent to a three-year low. The fall was amplified by its buyback record date, which brought additional selling pressure on top of the global technology rout. For Indian IT services companies that derive substantial revenue from AI-related projects with American clients, the Broadcom earnings report landed as a warning shot.

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan kept the company's full-year AI semiconductor guidance unchanged at "in excess of $100 billion," refusing to raise it despite market expectations. The signal was unmistakable: even the companies building the physical infrastructure of AI are not seeing infinite demand acceleration. Good is no longer enough.

## The Fed Factor

A stronger-than-expected US jobs report on Friday compounded the damage. Non-farm payrolls rose 172,000 against an 85,000 consensus, with prior months revised upward by a combined 93,000. Unemployment held at 4.3 percent. The combination of hot employment data and April CPI at 3.8 percent — the highest since May 2023 — pushed money markets to nearly fully price in a Federal Reserve rate hike by year-end.

According to the CME FedWatch tool, the probability of at least one rate hike in 2026 has jumped to 74.4 percent, up from 45.2 percent just a week ago. Rising US Treasury yields make richly valued technology stocks less attractive, and the AI trade had been among the most richly valued of all.

## What It Means for Indian Investors

For the roughly 15 crore Indian demat account holders — many of whom piled into IT and technology funds during the AI rally — the message is uncomfortable. The AI trade is not dead, but it is no longer a one-way bet. Broadcom's revenue is still growing at 48 percent year-over-year. Its AI chip revenue is still tripling. But at valuations of 65 times earnings and 25 times sales, the margin for disappointment is razor-thin.

Indian IT services firms face a secondary risk. If American hyperscalers — the Googles, Microsofts, and Anthropics of the world — begin rethinking their AI spending because costs are rising faster than returns, the downstream demand for Indian IT consulting and implementation work could slow before it ever fully materialised.

For now, the immediate concern is oil. Brent crude rose 4.3 percent to $97 a barrel on Monday as fresh Israeli strikes on Iran and Lebanon fuelled fears of wider conflict. India, which imports over 85 percent of its crude, is absorbing a double hit: global risk-off sentiment crushing its equity markets and rising energy costs pressuring its current account. The RBI's $50 billion dollar defense package, announced last Friday, has not yet stopped the rupee's slide.

The Broadcom earnings miss was not a catastrophe. It was a recalibration. But in a market priced for perfection, a recalibration can feel a lot like a crash.
